meta.title: Chinese Correlation Spine — anchor database
meta.method: Each record is one Chinese-dated anchor. date_ce is the Chinese event (translation, catalogue, sojourn, embassy). For a TAQ the hard bound is date_ce[1]. Lag is measured, never assumed zero; see spine.py lag.
meta.merge_note: Records from the BU project's CHINESE-SPINE.md catalogue are to be merged via `spine.py add` (schema-validated) — same field names by design.

anchors.indian_entity: Early Agama/Nikaya sutra corpus (An Shigao translations)
anchors.chinese_source: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji (Sengyou, c. 515) and Gaoseng Zhuan biographies
anchors.event: An Shigao, a Parthian monk, translates early sutras at Luoyang — the first dated translation activity in China
anchors.date_raw: Later Han, Jianning to Guanghe eras
anchors.firmness_reason: Translator's activity window is from later catalogues/biographies, not dated colophons
anchors.notes: Every text in his attributed corpus existed in India/Central Asia by the late 2nd c. CE at the latest. Individual attributions within the corpus are debated.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145
Zurcher, The Buddhist Conquest of China (1972)

anchors.indian_entity: Indian (Tianzhu) embassy to the Han court
anchors.chinese_source: Hou Han Shu (Book of the Later Han), Xiyu zhuan and imperial annals
anchors.event: Embassies from Tianzhu (India) reach the Han court by the sea route via Rinan in 159 and 161 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Dynastic annals record the arrivals; the sending Indian ruler is unnamed and unidentifiable
anchors.notes: Dates Indo-Chinese maritime contact, not any text. Useful as a floor for the transmission channel the later colophons presuppose.
references: Hou Han Shu, ch. 88 (Xiyu zhuan) and annals of Huan Di

anchors.chinese_source: Colophon preserved in Chu Sanzang Ji Ji (Sengyou, c. 515)
anchors.event: Lokaksema (Zhi Loujiachen) completes his translation (Daoxing Bore Jing, T.224) at Luoyang
anchors.date_raw: Later Han, Guanghe 2, 10th month (26 Oct 179 CE)
anchors.lag_basis: Composition conventionally placed c. 100 BCE-100 CE; the window is scholarly convention, not an independent anchor
anchors.firmness_reason: Colophon gives an exact day; corroborated by a C14-dated Gandhari Astasahasrika fragment (47-147 CE)
anchors.notes: Tier 1 anchor of the BU benchmark panel. The lag is carried for the record but excluded from the lag model (composition window not independently anchored).
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145
Falk & Karashima on the Bajaur Gandhari fragment

anchors.chinese_source: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji catalogue attribution to Lokaksema
anchors.event: Chinese translation (Banzhou Sanmei Jing, T.418) attributed to Lokaksema, dated 179 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Catalogue attribution and date are standard but the attribution has been questioned in modern scholarship
anchors.notes: One of the earliest Mahayana sutras attested anywhere, via China.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145
Harrison, The Samadhi of Direct Encounter (1990)

anchors.chinese_source: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji catalogue record of Zhi Qian's translation
anchors.event: Zhi Qian translates the Vimalakirti at the Wu court — the first Chinese version
anchors.date_raw: Cao Wei / Wu, Huangchu to Jiaping era
anchors.lag_basis: Composition estimates (c. 100 BCE-100 CE) are too soft to bound a lag honestly
anchors.firmness_reason: Translator's floruit (220s-250s) is biographically dated; no dated colophon for this version
anchors.notes: Kumarajiva's famous version (406) is a re-translation; the Zhi Qian version proves the text circulated two centuries earlier.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.chinese_source: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji attribution (partial translation, Zhi Qian era)
anchors.event: A partial Chinese translation attributed to the Zhi Qian circle is recorded by Sengyou
anchors.firmness_reason: Attribution in a catalogue compiled 260+ years later; no colophon date — a soft TAQ only
anchors.notes: Tier 2 (flagged) member of the BU benchmark panel; carried here with its softness explicit.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.chinese_source: Colophon preserved in Chu Sanzang Ji Ji
anchors.event: Dharmaraksa (Zhu Fahu) completes his translation (Zheng Fahua Jing, T.265); review finished 288
anchors.lag_basis: Composition of the sutra's core conventionally placed c. 50-150 CE on convergent scholarly estimates
anchors.firmness_reason: Colophon dated to the month; translation event is not in dispute
anchors.notes: Tier 1 anchor of the BU benchmark panel.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.chinese_source: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji record of Dharmaraksa's translation (Puyao Jing, T.186)
anchors.event: Dharmaraksa translates the Lalitavistara — his last reliably recorded work
anchors.lag_basis: The Sanskrit text is layered (core c. 100 CE, expansions to c. 300); a single lag for a layered text is not meaningful
anchors.firmness_reason: Translation year is catalogue-secure; what it dates is the core the translation knew, not every verse of the extant Sanskrit
anchors.notes: Tier 1 anchor of the BU benchmark panel, with the layering caveat carried in the panel itself.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.indian_entity: Chinese Buddhist canon as catalogued by Dao'an
anchors.chinese_source: Dao'an's Zongli Zhongjing Mulu (lost; quoted extensively by Sengyou)
anchors.event: Dao'an compiles the first catalogue of Chinese Buddhist translations, fixing which Indian texts had arrived by his day
anchors.firmness_reason: The catalogue itself is lost; its contents and date are known through Sengyou's quotations
anchors.notes: A master TAQ: every translation Dao'an lists existed by 374. Also the first Chinese source to voice doubts about anonymous 'sutras' — an early Chinese quality filter on the Indian material.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145 (quoting Dao'an)

anchors.chinese_source: Gaoseng Zhuan biography; Jin Shu annals
anchors.event: Kumarajiva, brought from Kucha, arrives at the Later Qin capital Chang'an and begins the imperially sponsored translation bureau
anchors.firmness_reason: Arrival and bureau activity (401-413) are dated in Chinese court and biographical records
anchors.notes: The bureau's dated output (402-413) is the densest cluster of exact TAQs in the whole spine.

anchors.chinese_source: Longshu Pusa Zhuan (Biography of Nagarjuna), translated in Kumarajiva's circle
anchors.event: A full legendary biography of Nagarjuna is translated at Chang'an — he is already a figure of the distant, storied past
anchors.lag_basis: A biography's translation dates the biography, not the life; no composition lag is computed from it
anchors.firmness_reason: Attribution to Kumarajiva himself is traditional; the bureau window 402-413 is secure
anchors.notes: Qualitative but real: by c. 405 Nagarjuna's life was already legend in the material reaching China — consistent with, though not proof of, a 2nd-3rd c. floruit.

anchors.chinese_source: Colophon of Kumarajiva's Miaofa Lianhua Jing (T.262)
anchors.event: Kumarajiva's re-translation of the Lotus Sutra at Chang'an
anchors.lag_basis: Lag is counted on the first-translation record (Dharmaraksa, 286), not on re-translations
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated colophon from the Chang'an bureau
anchors.notes: A re-translation TAQ is weaker evidence than a first translation (the text was already in China) but confirms the Sanskrit exemplar tradition was still live in the 400s.

anchors.chinese_source: Colophon of Kumarajiva's Zhong Lun (T.1564), Chang'an
anchors.event: Kumarajiva translates the Mulamadhyamakakarika with Pingala's commentary (Zhong Lun)
anchors.lag_basis: Nagarjuna's floruit c. 150-250 CE (Satavahana-era synchronisms and convergent scholarly placement)
anchors.firmness_reason: Bureau translation dated to the year in Chinese records
anchors.notes: The canonical lag case: Nagarjuna (fl. c. 150-250) to Kumarajiva (409) = roughly two centuries between an Indian master and his Chinese translation. Tier 1 anchor of the BU panel.

anchors.chinese_source: Maming Pusa Zhuan (Biography of Ashvaghosha), attributed to Kumarajiva
anchors.event: Ashvaghosha's biography is translated at Chang'an — like Nagarjuna, he is already a legendary figure of the past
anchors.firmness_reason: Attribution of the translation to Kumarajiva is traditional and has been doubted
anchors.notes: Pairs with the Buddhacarita translation (421) to bracket Ashvaghosha's Chinese reception in the early 5th c.

anchors.chinese_source: Faxian, Foguo Ji (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), with Chinese reign-era dating
anchors.event: Faxian travels India 399-414, spending c. 405-407 at Pataliputra in the Gupta realm of Candragupta II, copying Sanskrit manuscripts
anchors.firmness_reason: Itinerary is internally dated by Chinese era names; the Gupta synchronism is the standard reading of his Madhyadesa description
anchors.notes: Faxian never names the Gupta king — the synchronism is by date and place, which is exactly why it is strong: it is not a tradition, it is a timestamped eyewitness window onto c. 400 CE India.
references: Legge (tr.), A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms (1886)

anchors.chinese_source: Colophons of the Jiankang translation (Faxian with Buddhabhadra)
anchors.event: The Mahasamghika Vinaya manuscript Faxian obtained at Pataliputra is translated at Jiankang
anchors.lag_basis: Vinaya redaction history is stratified; no single composition window is defensible
anchors.firmness_reason: Translation window from colophons and Sengyou; year-level, not day-level
anchors.notes: Shows a complete Sanskrit Vinaya of an early school physically present in Gupta Pataliputra and in China by 418.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.chinese_source: Sengyou's catalogue (attribution to Baoyun); rival attribution to Dharmaksema in the Taisho preface
anchors.event: Fo Suoxing Zan, the Chinese Buddhacarita, is produced at Jiankang (Liu Song) by Baoyun (per Sengyou); the Taisho preface instead credits Dharmaksema
anchors.lag_basis: Ashvaghosha's floruit c. 78-150 CE, from the Kaniska court synchronism (TPQ = Kaniska era epoch, debated 78/127/144) and convergent placement c. 100 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Year 421 is catalogue-supported (Willemen), but the translator attribution is genuinely debated (Baoyun vs Dharmaksema)
anchors.notes: Tier 1 anchor of the BU benchmark panel ([78, 421]). The lag's lower end inherits the Kaniska-era debate: on the 127 or 144 epoch the lag shrinks by ~50-65 years.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145
Willemen (tr.), Buddhacarita: In Praise of Buddha's Acts (2009)

anchors.chinese_source: Biographical and catalogue records of Gunabhadra's Jiankang bureau
anchors.event: Gunabhadra (394-468) translates the Samyuktagama (Za Ahan Jing, T.99) at Jiankang
anchors.lag_basis: Agama redaction history is stratified; no single composition window is defensible
anchors.firmness_reason: Window from the translator's dated biography rather than a dated colophon
anchors.notes: A complete early-school Agama in Chinese by the 440s — a hard floor under the antiquity of the Agama tradition.
references: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography of Gunabhadra

anchors.chinese_source: Catalogue record of Gunabhadra's translation (T.670)
anchors.event: Gunabhadra translates the Lankavatara at Jiankang (an earlier lost Dharmaraksa version, c. 420-430, is also recorded)
anchors.firmness_reason: Year given in the catalogue tradition and consistent with the translator's dated activity
anchors.notes: The shortest solid lag in the set: a late Mahayana sutra reaching China within roughly a lifetime of composition — proof the lag is a distribution, not a constant. Tier 1 anchor of the BU panel.

anchors.indian_entity: Chinese Buddhist canon as catalogued by Sengyou
anchors.chinese_source: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji (T.2145)
anchors.event: Sengyou compiles the Chu Sanzang Ji Ji at Jiankang — the master bibliography of translations, preserving the early colophons this spine rests on
anchors.firmness_reason: Compilation year is approximate (c. 515, late Tianjian era), not colophon-exact
anchors.notes: A master TAQ for every translation it records — and the reason the 2nd-5th c. colophons survive at all.
references: Sengyou, Chu Sanzang Ji Ji, T.2145

anchors.chinese_source: Luoyang Qielan Ji (quoting Song Yun's itinerary) and Wei Shu
anchors.event: The Northern Wei court mission of Song Yun and Huisheng travels to Uddiyana and Gandhara and returns with 170 Sanskrit texts
anchors.firmness_reason: Court mission dated by era names; the itinerary survives quoted in a later work, not as an autograph
anchors.notes: A dated eyewitness window on Hephthalite-era Gandhara — political and monastic conditions c. 520.

anchors.chinese_source: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography; Luoyang Qielan Ji notice
anchors.event: Bodhidharma arrives in south China by sea and later appears at Luoyang
anchors.date_raw: Liang / Northern Wei, c. 520s (no era date in the earliest sources)
anchors.firmness_reason: Earliest sources give no year; 520/527 are later traditional assignments and the biography is heavily legendary
anchors.notes: Carried deliberately as a contested record: the tool grades, it does not launder legend into fact.

anchors.chinese_source: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography
anchors.event: Paramartha arrives at Guangzhou by sea with a cargo of Sanskrit manuscripts, summoned by the Liang emperor
anchors.firmness_reason: Year from his dated biography; biography is near-contemporary (Daoxuan, 7th c.)
anchors.notes: His translation bureau (546-569) and his Vasubandhu biography are two of the spine's most consequential Indian-chronology sources.

anchors.chinese_source: Paramartha's Suvarnasaptati translation (Jin Qishi Lun, T.2137) and his biography
anchors.event: Paramartha translates the Samkhyakarika with its commentary (Suvarnasaptati) in China; the Sanskrit exemplar had reached China in 546
anchors.lag_basis: Ishvarakrishna conventionally placed c. 350-450 CE; lag = translation window (557-569) minus composition window (350-450)
anchors.firmness_reason: The panel's TAQ 569 is the end of Paramartha's dated lifetime; the translation's exact year inside 557-569 is not colophon-fixed
anchors.notes: A Brahmanical (non-Buddhist) text anchored purely by a Buddhist translator's dated Chinese activity — the spine working across traditions. Tier 1 anchor of the BU panel.

anchors.chinese_source: Paramartha, Life of Vasubandhu (Posoupandou Fashi Zhuan, T.2049)
anchors.event: Paramartha composes/translates the earliest biography of Vasubandhu in China, placing him some generations in the past, brother of Asanga, under a king Vikramaditya of Ayodhya
anchors.lag_basis: The biography constrains Vasubandhu's era only through its internal synchronisms (a Vikramaditya, a king Baladitya) — identifications are the debate, so no lag is computed
anchors.firmness_reason: The main external evidence in the Vasubandhu dating debate (Frauwallner's 4th-c. reading vs the traditional 5th-c. one) is this single biographical tradition
anchors.notes: The classic case of Chinese evidence being load-bearing AND contested at once: the tool records the constraint and its contest, not a verdict.
references: Takakusu (tr.), 'The Life of Vasu-bandhu by Paramartha' (1904)

anchors.chinese_source: Da Tang Xiyu Ji (646) and Huili's biography of Xuanzang
anchors.event: Xuanzang travels India 629-645: studies at Nalanda under Shilabhadra, tours the kingdoms, attends Harsa's assemblies, returns to Chang'an with 657 Sanskrit texts
anchors.firmness_reason: Departure, itinerary and return (645) are dated in court records and his biography to the year
anchors.notes: The single richest dated eyewitness source for 7th-c. India. Zhenguan 19 = 645 is one of the converter's test cases.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, T.2087
Huili, Da Ci'en Si Sanzang Fashi Zhuan, T.2053

anchors.chinese_source: Da Tang Xiyu Ji and Xuanzang's biography
anchors.event: Xuanzang studies under Shilabhadra, the aged head of Nalanda, in the 630s; Shilabhadra was the pupil of Dharmapala
anchors.firmness_reason: The sojourn is dated; the biography's age for Shilabhadra (106) is hagiographic and is NOT used
anchors.notes: Anchors the Nalanda teacher-lineage (Dharmapala -> Shilabhadra -> Xuanzang) that Indian logic/epistemology chronology hangs from.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, T.2087
Huili, Da Ci'en Si Sanzang Fashi Zhuan, T.2053

anchors.chinese_source: Da Tang Xiyu Ji; Xuanzang biography; Tang annals
anchors.event: Xuanzang at Harsa's court: the Kanyakubja assembly and Prayaga festival, and his meeting with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa, Harsa's ally
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated eyewitness meeting, cross-checked by Harsa's own era-dated inscriptions (epoch 606)
anchors.notes: With the annals record of his death (647) this gives the [606, 647] bracket that anchors Bana's Harsacarita — the BU panel's tightest early two-sided interval.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, T.2087

anchors.indian_entity: Wang Xuance's first embassy to Magadha
anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang Shu and Xin Tang Shu, Tianzhu zhuan
anchors.event: Wang Xuance leads the Tang embassy to Harsa's Magadha and returns with an Indian ambassador's return mission
anchors.firmness_reason: Court annals record the embassy by reign year
anchors.notes: Diplomatic synchronism independent of the pilgrim record — two Chinese genres agreeing on Harsa's floruit.

anchors.indian_entity: Indian kingdoms as described in the Da Tang Xiyu Ji
anchors.chinese_source: Tang court record of the work's presentation
anchors.event: Xuanzang's Da Tang Xiyu Ji, his gazetteer of the 110+ Indian and Central Asian states he saw or heard of, is presented to Emperor Taizong
anchors.firmness_reason: Presentation year is court-dated
anchors.notes: Everything the Xiyu Ji describes as existing — kingdoms, monasteries, stupas, living teachers — is thereby dated to no later than 646, and its past-tense notices are TPQ-grade evidence for decline by then.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, T.2087 (presented 646)

anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang Shu and Xin Tang Shu, Tianzhu zhuan
anchors.event: Harsa dies without an heir (647); his usurping minister Arunasha attacks Wang Xuance's 648 embassy, which retaliates with Tibetan and Nepalese troops and captures him
anchors.firmness_reason: The 648 battle is annal-dated; the death year 647 is the standard inference (alive for the 643 embassy, dead before the 648 attack)
anchors.notes: Closes the [606, 647] Harsa bracket from the Chinese side. An Indian emperor's death year known only because a Chinese envoy was attacked — the spine in one anecdote.

anchors.chinese_source: Colophon of Xuanzang's Cheng Weishi Lun (T.1585)
anchors.event: Xuanzang compiles/translates the Cheng Weishi Lun at Chang'an, incorporating Vasubandhu's Trimsika and Vimsika with ten commentaries
anchors.lag_basis: Frauwallner dating of Vasubandhu (c. 316-396) from Paramartha's biography; the rival traditional dating (c. 400-480) would give lag [179, 259] instead
anchors.firmness_reason: Translation year is colophon-firm; the lag is excluded from the model because Vasubandhu's own window is the contested quantity
anchors.notes: A deliberately circularity-safe record: the TAQ is hard, the lag is flagged unusable precisely because it would assume the Vasubandhu date the spine is meant to test.

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (Record, sent home 691) and his pilgrim biographies
anchors.event: Yijing sails from Guangzhou (671), studies at Nalanda c. 675-685, returns to China 695 with some 400 Sanskrit texts
anchors.firmness_reason: Departure, sojourn and return are dated in his own works and court records
anchors.notes: His Record (written 691) is a dated snapshot of Indian Buddhism and Sanskrit learning in the generation after Xuanzang.
references: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, T.2125
Takakusu (tr.), A Record of the Buddhist Religion (1896)

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (Record of Buddhist Practices), chapter on Sanskrit grammar
anchors.event: Yijing reports that Bhartrihari — author of the Vakyapadiya and the Bhartrihari-shastra — died forty years before his Record (691), i.e. 651-652 CE, after seven times alternating between monk and lay life; he also calls him a contemporary of Dharmapala
anchors.date_raw: Record dated Tang, Tianshou 2 (691); death = 691 minus 'forty years'
anchors.firmness_reason: 'Forty years' is a round figure, and the Dharmapala-contemporaneity sits awkwardly with it (Dharmapala is usually placed c. 530-561) — yet this remains the sheet-anchor of Bhartrihari chronology
anchors.notes: Max Muller called Yijing's notice 'a new sheet-anchor in the chronology of Sanskrit literature'. It flatly contradicts the Indian tradition making Bhartrihari the brother of a 1st-c. BCE Vikramaditya — the canonical case of the Chinese record correcting an Indian traditional date. Some modern scholars argue for a 5th-c. Bhartrihari, which is why this is graded probable, not firm.
references: Takakusu (tr.), A Record of the Buddhist Religion (1896), pp. lvii, 181
Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, T.2125

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, chapter on Sanskrit grammar
anchors.event: Yijing reports Jayaditya, co-author (with Vamana) of the Kashikavrtti on Panini, died nearly thirty years before his Record
anchors.date_raw: Record dated 691; death = 691 minus 'nearly thirty years'
anchors.firmness_reason: Same round-number caveat as the Bhartrihari notice; the two notices corroborate each other's milieu
anchors.notes: Anchors the Kashikavrtti (and so a terminus for the whole Paninian commentarial tradition) to the mid-7th c. — from a Chinese pilgrim's grammar chapter, not from any Indian source.
references: Takakusu (tr.), A Record of the Buddhist Religion (1896), p. lvii

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan
anchors.event: Yijing names Dharmakirti among the recent masters who improved the science of logic (hetu) after Dinnaga and Jina
anchors.firmness_reason: A mention as an established authority by 691 is a real TAQ for his works, but says nothing tighter about his floruit
anchors.notes: Consistent with the standard c. 600-660 placement; the Chinese mention is one of the few non-Tibetan external checks on it.
references: Takakusu (tr.), A Record of the Buddhist Religion (1896)

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang's and Yijing's lineage statements (teacher of Shilabhadra; contemporary of Bhartrihari)
anchors.event: Xuanzang (630s) reports Dharmapala as his teacher Shilabhadra's teacher, already of the previous generation; Yijing calls him Bhartrihari's contemporary
anchors.firmness_reason: Generation-counting from dated pupils; the two Chinese notices (previous generation in the 630s; contemporary of a man who died 651) do not sit comfortably together
anchors.notes: The conventional c. 530-561 floruit is a construction from these Chinese lineage data plus Tibetan tradition — flagged here as generation-counting, the weakest link type in the spine.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, T.2087
Takakusu (tr.), A Record of the Buddhist Religion (1896)

anchors.indian_entity: Chinese Buddhist canon as catalogued in the Kaiyuan era
anchors.chinese_source: Zhisheng, Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu (T.2154)
anchors.event: Zhisheng compiles the Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu, the definitive Tang catalogue of the canon (2,487 works in 7,302 fascicles recorded as extant or known)
anchors.firmness_reason: Catalogue dated by its own preface to Kaiyuan 18 = 730 CE
anchors.notes: Master TAQ for the entire pre-730 translation corpus; also the source that retrospectively fixes many earlier translators' dates. Kaiyuan 18 = 730 is a converter test case.

anchors.chinese_source: Catalogue record of Shubhakarasimha's translation (with Yixing's commentary)
anchors.event: Shubhakarasimha, newly arrived from India, translates the Mahavairocana-sutra at Chang'an with Yixing
anchors.lag_basis: Tantric composition windows are too contested to bound a lag
anchors.firmness_reason: Year from the Tang catalogues and Yixing's biography; not a surviving dated colophon
anchors.notes: Marks the dated arrival of mature tantric Buddhism in China — a TAQ the Indian-side tantric chronology debate must respect.

anchors.chinese_source: Huichao, Wang Ocheonchukguk Jeon (Memoir of the Pilgrimage to the Five Kingdoms of India)
anchors.event: The Korean monk Huichao (Hyecho) travels India by sea and returns overland through Central Asia, describing the post-Harsa political map
anchors.firmness_reason: Dates reconstructed from the itinerary and era references; the manuscript (found at Dunhuang) is fragmentary
anchors.notes: A dated snapshot of India between Harsa and the Palas, from outside both the Indian and the Chinese-court traditions.
references: Huichao, Wang Ocheonchukguk Jeon (Dunhuang ms., P.3532)

anchors.chinese_source: Tang catalogues and Amoghavajra's memorials/lists of translations
anchors.event: Amoghavajra's court translation bureau produces its dated output of tantric texts (his own submitted lists survive)
anchors.firmness_reason: The bureau's activity window is court-dated; individual titles' years vary inside it
anchors.notes: Every tantric work in his lists existed in India (or its diaspora) by the mid-8th c. — a bulk TAQ for early tantric literature.

anchors.chinese_source: Catalogue prefaces and the record of Wukong's return (Yuanshao's preface)
anchors.event: Wukong goes to India with a Tang embassy (751), stays nearly forty years in Kashmir and Gandhara, is ordained, and returns to Chang'an (790) with Sanskrit texts
anchors.firmness_reason: Endpoints are recorded; the long sojourn's internal chronology is thin
anchors.notes: The last great dated Chinese eyewitness window on pre-Islamic Kashmir/Gandhara Buddhism.
references: Yuanshao, preface to Wukong's translations (in Kaiyuan-line catalogues)

anchors.indian_entity: Late Indian tantric texts (Song translation bureau)
anchors.chinese_source: Song catalogues and court records of the refounded translation bureau
anchors.event: The Northern Song refounds the imperial translation bureau (982); Indian and Central Asian monks (Dharmadeva/Faxian II, Tianxizai/Devashantika, Danapala) translate newly arrived Sanskrit manuscripts
anchors.firmness_reason: Bureau refounding is court-dated; the window covers the first translators' activity, individual titles vary
anchors.notes: The spine's far end: Sanskrit manuscripts were still physically travelling from India to China at the turn of the 11th c., dating the last stratum of Indian Buddhist literature by arrival.

anchors.chinese_source: Lidai Sanbao Ji (Fei Changfang, 597 CE); Da Tang Neidian Lu (Daoxuan, 664)
anchors.event: Sanghabhadra, translator of the Samantapasadika, places the 975th dot of the vinaya dotted record at Canton; the count, begun by Upali at the first pavarana after the parinirvana and handed down the Theravada vinaya lineage, implies parinirvana in 486 BCE
anchors.firmness_reason: The record is real but NOT independent: its custodian chain is the Theravada vinaya lineage itself, so its 486 BCE agrees with the Ceylon 218-year chronology because both are the same tradition's arithmetic (Pachow: the count needs a 3-dot adjustment to land on 483)
anchors.notes: Campaign case 1 verdict: NO BITE as an independent correction. Carried so the tool refuses to count it as a second witness for the long chronology.
references: Daoxuan, Da Tang Neidian Lu, T.2149
Pachow, A Study of the Dotted Record
Bechert (ed.), Die Datierung des historischen Buddha

anchors.chinese_source: Hou Hanshu, ch. 88 (Western Regions)
anchors.event: The Hou Hanshu Kushan account, based on reports current to c. 125 CE, names Kujula Kadphises and his son (Vima Takto) but not Kanishka, and gives no Kushan regnal date
anchors.date_raw: Report horizon c. Jianwu to Yongning era reports, compiled in Hou Hanshu
anchors.firmness_reason: Argument from silence/report horizon: suggests Kanishka had not risen (or was unknown at court) by c. 125, but the account's India coverage is thin
anchors.notes: Campaign case 2: soft lower bound on the era epoch; combined with the Bodiao entry it confines the epoch to c. 125-165 and excludes 78 CE.

anchors.chinese_source: Sanguozhi, ch. 3 (annals of Emperor Ming of Wei)
anchors.event: The king of the Da Yuezhi, Bodiao (Vasudeva I), sends tribute; the Wei emperor grants him the title King of the Da Yuezhi Intimate with Wei
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; the bound it generates depends on the Bodiao = Vasudeva I identification (a Vasudeva II has been proposed)
anchors.notes: Vasudeva I's era-dated inscriptions run years 64-98; his being on the throne in 229 excludes a 78 CE era epoch (which would put 229 in era year 151) and is consistent with 127 or 144.

anchors.chinese_source: Kumarajiva bureau translation records (Biography of Asvaghosa, T.2046)
anchors.event: Kumarajiva's Chang'an bureau translates the Biography of Asvaghosa, c. 405 CE - by then he is a legendary, biographised figure
anchors.firmness_reason: Bureau attribution and period are standard; the biography's legendary maturity is an inference about floruit, not a date
anchors.notes: Campaign case 3: supports a floruit well before 400; working floruit c. 100-200 with the Kaniska relation (era-dependent).
references: Chu Sanzang Ji Ji / Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu records for T.2046

anchors.lag_basis: Composition c. 100-200 CE on the Kanishka-relation placement; the window is era-dependent, not independent of the synchronism tradition
anchors.chinese_source: Dharmaksema translation record (Fo suoxing zan, T.192)
anchors.event: Dharmaksema translates the Buddhacarita into Chinese, c. 412-421 CE (Northern Liang)
anchors.firmness_reason: Translation window is the standard catalogue dating for Dharmaksema's Northern Liang activity
anchors.notes: Hard late bound for Asvaghosa; cf. spine C10.

anchors.lag_basis: Standard composition range c. 150-250 CE (spine lag table); range is scholarly convention, carried but the TAQ itself is the load-bearing datum
anchors.chinese_source: Kumarajiva bureau colophon, Chang'an (Zhong lun, T.1564)
anchors.event: Kumarajiva translates the Mulamadhyamakarika with Pingala's commentary in 409 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Court-documented translation bureau output with reign-era date
anchors.notes: Campaign case 4 verdict CORRECTED: closes the hagiographic 400-600-year lifespan placements; working floruit c. 150-250. Cf. spine C8.

anchors.chinese_source: Paramartha, Life of Vasubandhu (T.2049), composed c. 563-569, preserved only in Chinese
anchors.event: Paramartha composes/transmits the Life of Vasubandhu: Purusapura origin, brother Asanga, death at Ayodhya aged 80; its internal nirvana-interval figures are tradition arithmetic, not record
anchors.firmness_reason: Author's own dates are Chinese-recorded and the text survives only in Chinese; its factual content is one inferential step from record and its interval numbers are demonstrably unreliable
anchors.notes: Campaign case 5: primary biographical source for the pair; use its facts, refuse its numbers.

anchors.chinese_source: Bodhiruci translation record, Luoyang (T.1522)
anchors.event: Bodhiruci translates Vasubandhu's Dasabhumika commentary, c. 508-512 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Standard catalogue dating for Bodhiruci's Luoyang activity
anchors.notes: Earliest firm TAQ in the Vasubandhu stack; pushes his floruit no later than the later 5th century on any plausible lag. Cf. spine C18.

anchors.chinese_source: Paramartha translation record (T.1559)
anchors.event: Paramartha translates the Abhidharmakosa-bhasya, 563-567 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Translator's activity is independently dated (Paramartha 499-569, in China from 546)
anchors.notes: Cf. spine C16. Xuanzang's retranslation 651-654 (T.1558) is a catalogue cross-check, not a tighter bound.

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang translation record (T.1628)
anchors.event: Xuanzang translates Dignaga's Nyayamukha in 649 CE; Dignaga's corpus was already curriculum material during Xuanzang's Indian study years (630s-640s)
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated output of Xuanzang's court translation bureau
anchors.notes: Campaign case 6. Note: the spine catalogue's shorthand 'Alambanapariksa translated by Xuanzang 632' should read as his in-India study period; his translations are 645-664 (Alambanapariksa bureau translation 657).

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan (sent to China 691)
anchors.event: Yijing lists Dharmakirti among the 'recent' masters and reports his works taught near Nalanda c. 665-670; Xuanzang (in India 629-645) never mentions him; no work of Dharmakirti was translated into Chinese in the Tang
anchors.firmness_reason: Positive mention is a dated eyewitness-generation report; the bracket's lower half rests on Xuanzang's silence, an argumentum ex silentio graded accordingly
anchors.notes: Campaign case 6 verdict BOUNDED: fame by 691 firm; floruit c. 550-660 all compatible with the Chinese frame once the silence is priced. Cf. spine C28.
references: Frauwallner, Landmarks in the History of Indian Logic

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan, grammar chapter (sent to China 691)
anchors.event: Yijing names Bhartrhari's works, makes him a contemporary of Dharmapala, and states 'it is forty years since his death' - implying death c. 651-652 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: Firm as a record of what Yijing reports; Probable as history (Frauwallner-line pushback and the two-Bhartrhari escape hatch are documented in the spine)
anchors.notes: Campaign case 7 (calibration): verdict CORRECTED. Muller: 'a new sheet-anchor in the chronology of Sanskrit literature.' Cf. spine C26.

anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu accounts
anchors.event: Harsha ('king of Magadha') sends an embassy to Taizong; the Tang reply mission under Li Yibiao with Wang Xuance is in India 643-645; Xuanzang received at Harsha's court, Kannauj assembly 643
anchors.firmness_reason: Court annal record of received embassies, reign-era dated at every step
anchors.notes: Cf. spine C19/C21.
references: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu zhuan

anchors.chinese_source: Tang annals and the excerpted remains of Wang Xuance's account
anchors.event: Wang Xuance's second mission (dispatched 647) finds Harsha dead and a usurper (Arunasva) enthroned; Wang defeats and captures the usurper in 648 with Tibetan and Nepalese troops
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic sequence; only the usurper's name/identity is Probable. No Indian source dates Harsha's death at all
anchors.notes: Campaign case 8 (calibration) verdict CORRECTED: death 647; with the Indian accession (606) gives the two-sided reign bracket [606, 647]. Cf. spine C22.
references: Levi, Les missions de Wang Hiuan-ts'e

anchors.chinese_source: Xin Tang shu, Western Regions (Kashmir entry)
anchors.event: Embassy from Candrapida of Kashmir reaches Xuanzong's court requesting aid against the Arabs and Tibet
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic record of a received embassy; the name equation Zhentuoluobili = Candrapida is standard
anchors.notes: Campaign case 9: Kalhana's received chronology has Candrapida dead by 688 - the annals put him on the throne in 713.

anchors.chinese_source: Xin Tang shu / Tang edicts (Kashmir entry)
anchors.event: Tang court invests Candrapida by edict as King of Kashmir (720); a further edict (722) praises Kashmir for provisioning Tang troops in Gilgit
anchors.firmness_reason: Court edicts recorded in the annals with reign-era dates
anchors.notes: Cunningham's computation: by this investiture Kalhana's chronology is in error by exactly 31 years for Candrapida.
references: Cunningham, Ancient Geography / Rajatarangini chronology discussions

anchors.chinese_source: Xin Tang shu, Western Regions (Kashmir entry)
anchors.event: Muduobi (Muktapida), Candrapida's younger brother, sends the envoy Wuliduo requesting investiture, offering troops and a temple by the Mahapadma lake; invested by the Tang court
anchors.date_raw: Xuanzong reign; Stein dates the embassy after the Baltistan operations of 736-747
anchors.firmness_reason: The annalistic entry is firm; its exact year is Stein's inference from the Baltistan-expedition context, and Muduobi = Muktapida is Stein's identification ('beyond doubt' in his judgement)
anchors.notes: Campaign case 9: corrected placement Lalitaditya c. 724/725-760/761, against Kalhana-derived 699-736.

anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu (Old Book of Tang), Nepal (Nipoluo) account; Old Tibetan Annals frame
anchors.event: After the usurpation by his uncle Visnugupta, Narendradeva flees to Tibet; the Tibetans re-establish him on the Nepalese throne (641), making Nepal a Tibetan client; Nepal supplies 7,000 troops to Wang Xuance's 648 campaign and the Tangshu describes Narendradeva as reigning king in information current to c. 648
anchors.date_raw: Restoration pegged to 641 (Zhenguan 15 era frame; Tibetan annals place the Nepal intervention in the early 640s)
anchors.firmness_reason: Event sequence is annalistic and the Tibetan record concurs; the exact year 641 is the standard scholarly peg within 641-643 rather than a year stated in so many words, and the Tangshu narrative compresses the inscriptional Jishnugupta/Dhruvadeva tangle
anchors.notes: Campaign case 10 verdict CORRECTED: the vaimsavali chronology supplies no absolute date for this segment; the Tang/Tibetan peg is the only one.

anchors.indian_entity: Huna king of Gandhara (Song Yun's audience)
anchors.chinese_source: Song Yun's itinerary, preserved in Luoyang qielan ji (c. 547)
anchors.event: Song Yun (embassy 518-522) meets the Huna king ruling Gandhara - cruel, unbelieving, on campaign - whose people conquered Gandhara two generations earlier; the Kaniska stupa still stands
anchors.date_raw: Northern Wei, Shengui 1 to Zhengguang 3 (518-522); audience c. 520
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation; the king is unnamed and the Mihirakula identification, though standard, is an inference
anchors.notes: Campaign case 11 verdict CORROBORATED: 520 falls inside Mihirakula's epigraphic floruit (c. 515-542); 'two generations since the conquest' gives a conquest horizon c. 460-490. Cf. spine C14.

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu ji (646)
anchors.event: Xuanzang narrates Mihirakula's persecution and his defeat/capture by the Gupta king Baladitya, but places him 'several hundred years' before his own time - the actual gap is c. 100 years
anchors.firmness_reason: The narrative corroborates the Baladitya-defeat tradition, but the stated interval is a demonstrable Chinese-side error (c. 100 years reported as several hundred); carried as a reliability flag, not a bound
anchors.notes: Campaign case 11: the campaign's clearest proof that pilgrim-reported intervals are tradition, while pilgrim observation is record.

anchors.chinese_source: Faxian, Foguo ji (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms)
anchors.event: Faxian in India 399-414 (three years at Pataliputra): a prosperous, lightly governed paramount kingdom centred at Pataliputra; the king is never named
anchors.firmness_reason: Itinerary is internally dated and firm; the identification of the unnamed king's frame with Candragupta II (r. c. 375-415, inscriptions to Gupta year 93 = 412) is inferential
anchors.notes: Campaign case 12 (corroboration test) verdict CORROBORATED: the frame holds; graded Probable because an unnamed king's prosperity would corroborate a wrong reign almost as smoothly. Cf. spine C11.

anchors.chinese_source: Song annals (Song Shi / Song Huiyao), Zhulian (Chola) file
anchors.event: First Chola mission reaches the Song court; the sending king is named Lo-ts'a-lo-ts'a (Rajaraja). Dispatched in Rajaraja's name one to two sailing seasons earlier; he died in 1014, months before the arrival
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation phonetically transparent
anchors.notes: Campaign case 13 verdict CORROBORATED. The Song file also preserves Srivijaya's earlier misrepresentation of Chola as its dependency, which this mission corrected at court.

anchors.chinese_source: Song annals, Zhulian (Chola) file
anchors.event: Chola mission from Shi-lo-cha Yin-to-lo Chu-lo (Sri Raja Indra Chola = Rajendra I) reaches the Song court
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation transparent
anchors.notes: Falls inside Rajendra's inscriptionally dated sole reign (1014-1044): exact corroboration.

anchors.chinese_source: Song annals, Zhulian (Chola) file
anchors.event: Mission of seventy merchants from Ti-hua-kia-lo (Deva Kulottunga = Kulottunga I) received at the Song court; 81,800 strings of copper cash given for its tribute goods
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation standard
anchors.notes: Independently confirms Kulottunga I (accession 1070 by the inscriptional computation) on the throne in 1077.

anchors.indian_entity: Srivijaya (Fo-shih) as a Buddhist learning centre
anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, travel memoir and Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan
anchors.event: Yijing spends six months in Fo-shih (Srivijaya) in 671: a fortified royal city with more than a thousand monks, learning ranked with Madhyadesa's; he studies Sanskrit grammar there and recommends it to Chinese students
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation - the spine's zero-lag class
anchors.notes: Campaign case 14 verdict BOUNDED: a mature Srivijaya existed in 671, eleven years before its first surviving inscription (Kedukan Bukit, 682); the rise is bounded to the 660s at the latest.

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, travel memoir
anchors.event: Yijing passed Mo-lo-yu (Malayu) as a separate country in 673; by his return stay in Srivijaya (685-689) he records that Mo-lo-yu 'has become Fo-shih'
anchors.firmness_reason: Two dated eyewitness observations bracketing the event
anchors.notes: Annexation of Malayu bracketed to (673, 689] - Srivijaya's first datable act of expansion.

anchors.chinese_source: Baolin Zhuan (801), lost; known through quotation and the list it standardised
anchors.event: The Baolin Zhuan fixes the canonical list of 28 Indian patriarchs ending Prajnatara (27) - Bodhidharma (28), reopening the line the Fu Fazang Yinyuan Zhuan (472) had closed at Simha's beheading by inserting Basiasita, Punyamitra and Prajnatara
anchors.firmness_reason: The fixing of the list at 801 is the standard scholarly account, but the text is lost and the list is known through later quotation
anchors.notes: First attestation of Prajnatara in any source. The names between Simha and Bodhidharma are the least stable segment across competing Tang lists (Lidai Fabao Ji c. 775 differs).

anchors.chinese_source: Luoyang Qielan Ji notice (547); Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography (645-667)
anchors.event: Bodhidharma's defensible floruit: present in Luoyang 516-526, dead before 534; arrival best supported under the Liu Song (by the 470s) per Daoxuan
anchors.firmness_reason: Two independent near-contemporary witnesses; the window rests on the Yongning Temple inference and Daoxuan's pre-534 death horizon
anchors.notes: Refines and bounds the contested seed record bodhidharma-arrival-c520: the 520/527 arrival dates are later traditional assignments; 527 is falsified by this window.

anchors.chinese_source: Near-contemporary biographical records; East Mountain community tradition
anchors.event: Floruit of Daoxin (580-651), fourth Chinese node of the Lengjia chart
anchors.firmness_reason: Attested in near-contemporary records; dates conventional in the biographical tradition and consistent with the Hongren succession
anchors.notes: Daoxin (b. 580) to Hongren (b. 601) is the first normal generational interval (~21 years) in the chart.

anchors.chinese_source: Epitaph for Faru (638-689), dated inscription
anchors.event: The epitaph for Faru gives the first lineage succession of any kind: Bodhidharma - Huike - Sengcan - Daoxin - Hongren - Faru. Before 689 no source arranges these men as a succession
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated inscription; the lineage claim's first appearance is fixed by the stone's own date
anchors.notes: TAQ on the lineage idea itself: the chart is a late-7th-century artefact, ~160 years after Bodhidharma's death.

anchors.chinese_source: Gaoseng Zhuan / Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biographical tradition and translation catalogues
anchors.event: Death of Gunabhadra (394-468), the Lankavatara translator — the terminus that constrains the Lengjia Shizi Ji chart: any personal discipleship of Bodhidharma under Gunabhadra must end by 468
anchors.firmness_reason: Death year from the dated biographical tradition for a translator whose activity (435 arrival, 443 Lankavatara) is catalogue-anchored; not itself a dated colophon
anchors.notes: Chart constraint, not a text TAQ: with the 527-arrival tradition it forces a >=59-year gap between discipleship and arrival; with the Liu Song arrival (<=479) it forces arrival by the 460s.
references: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography of Gunabhadra

anchors.chinese_source: Multiple biographical notices; Faru epitaph (689) from inside his community
anchors.event: Floruit of Hongren (601-674; some sources 602-675), fifth Chinese node of the Lengjia chart
anchors.firmness_reason: Multiple independent attestations plus a dated inscription (689) by his disciple's circle; the first node after Gunabhadra where cross-dating fully works
anchors.notes: Some sources give 602-675; the one-year variance is recorded rather than resolved.

anchors.chinese_source: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography of Huike; later biographical tradition
anchors.event: Death of Huike (487-593), Bodhidharma's disciple and recipient of the 4-fascicle Lankavatara per Daoxuan
anchors.firmness_reason: Death era consistent across the biographical tradition; the implied 107-year lifespan (487-593) is longevity inflation and is not load-bearing
anchors.notes: Chart node 2 of the Lengjia line. Daoxuan has his arm lost to bandits; the self-severing version is first epigraphically attested on a stele of 798.

anchors.chinese_source: Baolin Zhuan (801) patriarch list; first extant narratives Zutang Ji (952) and Jingde Chuandeng Lu (1004)
anchors.event: First attestation of Prajnatara, Bodhidharma's putative teacher and 27th Indian patriarch: an ATTESTATION record, not a date for a life. No attestation exists in Tanlin, Daoxuan, the Lengjia Shizi Ji, the Fu Fazang list (472), or any Indian, Tibetan, Central Asian or non-Chan Chinese source
anchors.firmness_reason: The figure is attested only inside Chan lineage literature and only from 801, ~270 years after Bodhidharma's death; graded contested as a person, firm as an attestation date
anchors.notes: Default verdict of the Case 16 build: a lineage construction at the seam where the Fu Fazang list had declared the transmission extinct. A mid-9th-c. Nalanda namesake (folios preserved in Japan via Enchin) is unconnected. The female identification is a modern conjecture (Benson 2008).

anchors.chinese_source: Later Chan biographical tradition
anchors.event: Traditional death year of Sengcan, third node of the Lengjia chart after Bodhidharma and Huike
anchors.firmness_reason: Almost no independent attestation; the Huike-Sengcan link itself is flagged as tenuous in the scholarship (Whalen Lai). Carried with the grade shown, not dropped
anchors.notes: The chart's weakest node: a death year with no documented life. His 606 death, 13 years after Huike's, creates the downstream generational squeeze analysed in the Case 16 build.

anchors.chinese_source: Yang Xuanzhi, Luoyang Qielan Ji (547)
anchors.event: Yongning Temple built 516 and destroyed by fire 534; Yang Xuanzhi's notice places Bodhidharma admiring its stupa in the intact temple, bounding his Luoyang presence to 516-526 on Broughton's reading
anchors.firmness_reason: Temple construction/destruction are court-record dates; the sighting window is an inference from the gazetteer's description of the intact temple
anchors.notes: The hardest single terminus in the Bodhidharma dossier: falsifies the 527 Liang-arrival tradition, which postdates this entire window.

anchors.chinese_source: Duarte Barbosa, The Book of Duarte Barbosa (composed c. 1516-1518) — first written record of the legend
anchors.event: Barbosa records that a Malabar king ('Chirimay Perumal') was converted by Moorish traders, sailed to Mecca and died there or en route, his kingdom partitioned — and dates the event 'more than 600 years before our time', i.e. c. 900 CE. No Prophet, no moon-splitting, no Malik ibn Dinar
anchors.firmness_reason: The legend existed in oral circulation by c. 1516 (firm); the composition window of Barbosa's book is approximate, hence probable for the record as dated
anchors.notes: TAQ for the LEGEND, and a synchronism against its modern form: the earliest witness dates the conversion to c. 900 and knows nothing of the 629 CE / Prophet's-lifetime synchronism, which is a later layer.
references: Barbosa, The Book of Duarte Barbosa (c. 1516-1518)
More, J. B. P., on the Portuguese notices of the legend

anchors.indian_entity: Cheraman Perumal conversion legend (full Malik ibn Dinar cycle)
anchors.chinese_source: Zainuddin Makhdum II, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin (Arabic, completed c. 1583) — first full devotional telling
anchors.event: The full cycle exists in writing: the pilgrims en route to Adam's Foot, the moon-splitting narration, the king's secret departure and death abroad, his letters, and Malik ibn Dinar's party founding mosques at Kodungallur and the named ports. Zainuddin himself dates the conversion to two hundred years after the Prophet (c. 820s), NOT to the Prophet's lifetime
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated, extant, authored text — the standard first history of Kerala by a Keralite
anchors.notes: TAQ for the developed legend. Its internal dating (c. 820s) is the legend's own earliest full-text chronology and contradicts the 629 CE date now displayed at the mosque.
references: Zainuddin Makhdum II, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin (c. 1583), trans. Nainar (1942)
More, J. B. P., on the Tuhfat's dating of the conversion

anchors.chinese_source: Ibn Battuta, Rihla — eyewitness account of his Malabar sojourn, 1342-1347
anchors.event: Describes mosques in every Malabar port town, named qadis at Calicut and Kollam, the cathedral mosque at Hili (Ezhimala) enriched by sailors' vows, and a Muslim shah bandar governing Calicut's port — Malabar Islam as a long-established institution
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness travel account, internally consistent with the 14th-century mosque epigraphy of Kozhikode (Kuttichira)
anchors.notes: Terminus: Malabar mosques are FIRM by the 1340s. Battuta records no foundation legend for Kodungallur and no 629 tradition.
references: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, Gibb translation, Malabar chapters

anchors.indian_entity: Joseph Rabban and the Jewish guild (Anjuvannam) of Kodungallur
anchors.chinese_source: Jewish copper plates of Cochin — Old Malayalam (Vattezhuthu with Grantha) royal charter of Bhaskara Ravi Varma (local epigraphy)
anchors.event: Bhaskara Ravi grants Joseph Rabban the rights of the Anjuvannam merchant guild and aristocratic privileges at Muyirikkottu (Kodungallur) — a chartered Jewish merchant lordship at the old Chera capital
anchors.date_raw: 38th regnal year of Bhaskara Ravi Varma
anchors.firmness_reason: Epigraphic consensus (Narayanan 1972 and successors) dates the plates c. 1000 CE via Bhaskara Ravi's accession c. 962; the community's traditional date is 379 CE
anchors.notes: Web anchor for the Kodungallur node: the plates are genuine, their traditional date overshoots the epigraphic date by ~620 years — the same tradition-vs-attestation gap shape as the Cheraman mosque claim (629 vs 11th-12th-c. fabric). Jewish presence on the coast is independently firm by 849 (Hebrew signatures on the Quilon plates).
references: Narayanan, M. G. S., Cultural Symbiosis in Kerala (1972); Perumals of Kerala (1996/2013)

anchors.chinese_source: Arabic foundation inscription (copper slab) preserved in the Madayi Mosque (local epigraphy as reported in the Kerala survey literature)
anchors.event: Foundation inscription dates the Madayi Mosque to Hijra 518 — the earliest dated mosque-foundation inscription in Kerala
anchors.firmness_reason: Reported consistently across the survey literature; no modern epigraphic edition was available to the build
anchors.notes: Mosque foundations on the Malabar coast become epigraphically visible in the 12th century. The date 1124 is sometimes misattributed in polemical literature to the Kodungallur (Cheraman) mosque, which has no dated foundation inscription.
references: Malabar Muslims / Mappila survey literature on the Madayi inscription

anchors.indian_entity: Settled Muslim community on India's west coast (Saymur/Chaul)
anchors.chinese_source: Al-Masudi, Muruj al-Dhahab (completed 943, revised 956), reporting his Indian sojourn of c. 915-916
anchors.event: Masudi reports some 10,000 bayasira (locally born Muslims) at Saymur (Chaul, Konkan coast) with ordinary and Friday mosques, protected by the Hindu king — a settled, second-generation, mosque-building Muslim community under Hindu rule
anchors.firmness_reason: Eyewitness-grade traveller report, but the named town is Saymur on the Konkan coast, NOT Malabar proper; the figure of 10,000 is a traveller's round number
anchors.notes: Bounds the regional pattern: by c. 915 mosque-building Muslim settlement under Hindu kings is normal on the west coast north of Malabar. It does not attest Malabar itself, and Masudi tells no convert-king story.
references: Al-Masudi, Muruj al-Dhahab wa Ma'adin al-Jawahir (943/956)

anchors.indian_entity: Muslim burial at Panthalayani Kollam, Malabar Coast
anchors.chinese_source: Arabic tombstone inscription outside the Juma mosque, Panthalayani Kollam (local epigraphy as reported in the Kerala survey literature)
anchors.event: Tombstone records the death of a Muslim (ibn Udthorman) in Hijra 166 — a Muslim buried on the Malabar coast, implying a burying community
anchors.firmness_reason: Reading circulates through secondary survey literature, not a modern epigraphic edition; AH 166 = 782-783 CE (repeatedly misprinted as '752 CE' in the secondary literature — a conversion error)
anchors.notes: If the reading holds, this is the earliest dated Muslim presence on the coast, two-thirds of a century before the Quilon plates. Grade is explicitly hostage to a critical re-edition of the stone.
references: Malabar Muslims / Mappila survey literature on the Panthalayani tombstone
Heritage: Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies in Archaeology 8.1 (2020) — prints the erroneous '752 CE' conversion

anchors.indian_entity: Muslim community of Kollam (Quilon), Malabar Coast
anchors.chinese_source: Quilon (Tarisapalli) copper plates — Chera royal charter of Ayyan Adikal under Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, witness plate (local epigraphy; the correlation source here is epigraphic, not Chinese)
anchors.event: Eleven Muslim witnesses sign, in Kufic Arabic, a royal charter granting privileges to the Christian Tarisapalli church at Kollam, alongside witnesses signing in Pahlavi and Hebrew — a settled Muslim community of charter-witnessing standing exists at Kollam
anchors.date_raw: 5th regnal year of Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara (Kollam era 24/25)
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated royal charter, extant plates; the standard epigraphic dating of the Tarisapalli grant
anchors.notes: Earliest FIRM attestation of a Muslim community on the Malabar coast. The signatures attest a community, not a mosque building; no mosque at Kollam or Kodungallur is dated by this document.
references: Quilon Syrian copper plates (849 CE), plate 5 witness signatures
Narayanan, M. G. S., Perumals of Kerala (1996/2013)

anchors.indian_entity: Kollam (Kulam Mali) in the Arab-Chinese sea trade
anchors.chinese_source: Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (Accounts of China and India), compiled 851, attributed to the merchant Sulaiman — an Arabic witness to the China run, held in the spine as the traveller-record class
anchors.event: Describes the working route Siraf-Muscat-Kulam Mali (Kollam), with Chinese ships paying heavy port dues at Kollam — Arab shipping serves Malabar as a mature entrepot system
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated compilation; the itinerary is first-hand merchant reporting
anchors.notes: Attests Arab TRADE presence and Kollam's role. It does NOT mention a Muslim community, a mosque, or a convert king in Malabar — a registered negative for the Cheraman claim.
references: Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851), Ferrand (1922) / Mackintosh-Smith (2014) editions

anchors.chinese_source: Xi'an Stele (781), corroborated in outline by Tang Huiyao fasc. 49
anchors.event: Alopen arrives at Chang'an from Daqin carrying scriptures and images; received by Fang Xuanling; the scriptures are translated in the imperial library
anchors.firmness_reason: Retrospective by 146 years on the stele; no contemporary Tang document records the arrival itself, though the 638 edict and the church's Tang presence are independently recorded
anchors.indian_entity: Alopen's mission — first documented Church of the East arrival in China
anchors.notes: Dates the ARRIVAL of the Church of the East in China — a transmission event. It attests the institution that carried the Thomas tradition east; it is not evidence about Thomas (1st c.).

anchors.chinese_source: Takht-i-Bahi Kharoshthi inscription (NON-CHINESE external anchor; this field carries the dating record per schema)
anchors.date_raw: Era year 103, regnal year 26 (era unnamed in the inscription)
anchors.event: Inscription dated in era year 103 and in Gondophares' 26th regnal year. On the standard identification of the unnamed era with the Azes era (= Vikrama era, year 1 = 57 BCE), year 103 = 46 CE and accession falls c. 20 CE
anchors.firmness_reason: The inscription is contemporary and names the king, but the absolute year rests entirely on identifying its unnamed era with Azes/Vikrama — Bivar (Encyclopaedia Iranica) treats the identification as settled; Robert Senior's alternative chronology reassigns the inscription to a later Gondophares
anchors.indian_entity: Gondophares I, Indo-Parthian king (the 'Gudnaphar' of the Acts of Thomas)
anchors.notes: Load-bearing anchor for the Acts of Thomas' Gondophares (reign c. 20-46 CE on the standard reading). Caveats: 'Gondophares' later became a dynastic title (Gondophares IV Sases, mid-to-late 1st c.), so the name alone does not fix which bearer an undated text means; his brother Gad in the Acts matches Gadana/Gad among the subordinate names on his coinage. Proposed as a non-Chinese external anchor, on the same logic as the Aihole prasasti in the BU benchmark panel.
references: Senior, 'More Gondophares, Less Azes', Oriental Numismatic Society Occasional Paper 25 (1991)

aliases: Daqin Jingjiao Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing pillar
anchors.chinese_source: Luoyang Jingjiao pillar inscription (recovered at Luoyang, published from 2006)
anchors.event: Stone pillar erected at Luoyang carrying the Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing text with a Syriac inscription naming East Syriac clergy — a second dated Jingjiao monument after the Xi'an Stele
anchors.firmness_reason: Self-dated pillar; recovered and published only in 2006, so the specialist literature is younger than for the Xi'an Stele
anchors.indian_entity: Jingjiao community at Luoyang (Daqin Jingjiao Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing pillar)
anchors.notes: The closest thing to a dated Jingjiao colophon-monument after 781. Its text is doctrinal (Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing); no Thomas material.
references: Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937), for the text's Dunhuang witness

anchors.chinese_source: Quilon (Tarisapalli) copper plates (NON-CHINESE external anchor; this field carries the dating record per schema)
anchors.date_raw: 5th regnal year of the Chera king Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara
anchors.event: Ayyan Adikal, chief of Kollam, grants land and privileges to the Tarisapalli church under the Persian merchant Maruvan Sapir Iso; the witness plate carries signatures in Pahlavi, Kufic Arabic and Judeo-Persian
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated by the regnal year of an epigraphically anchored Chera king; the plates survive; the Pahlavi witness signatures were edited by Cereti (2009)
anchors.indian_entity: Tarisapalli church, Kollam (Quilon) — East Syriac-linked Christian community in Kerala
anchors.notes: Proves a chartered, Persian-linked Christian church on the Malabar coast by 849 — and nothing about its founder. Community tradition associates the migration behind the grant with Mar Sabor and Mar Proth (arrival c. 825), but the plates name Maruvan Sapir Iso; the identification is traditional, not epigraphic.
references: Cereti, 'The Pahlavi Signatures on the Quilon Copper Plates' (2009)

aliases: Taizong edict on the Daqin religion
anchors.chinese_source: Edict text preserved in Tang Huiyao fasc. 49 (compiled 961) and quoted on the Xi'an Stele (781)
anchors.event: Emperor Taizong's edict approves propagation of the Daqin (Jingjiao) religion and authorises a temple in the Yining ward of Chang'an with twenty-one monks
anchors.firmness_reason: Edict text survives in a Song-compiled Tang institutional history and on the 781 stele; two carriers, neither contemporary paper
anchors.indian_entity: Imperial authorisation of Jingjiao in Tang China
anchors.notes: The earliest Chinese state document on Christianity. It names the religion and its Daqin origin; it does not name Thomas or any apostle.

aliases: Bosi si to Daqin si edict
anchors.chinese_source: Edict of Tianbao 4, preserved in Tang Huiyao / Tang institutional records
anchors.event: Imperial edict renames the religion's temples from Bosi si ('Persian temples') to Daqin si ('Daqin temples') in the two capitals and all prefectures, on the stated ground that the religion originates in Daqin, not Persia
anchors.firmness_reason: Edict text preserved in Tang institutional compilations; consistent with the stele's account of the church's status
anchors.indian_entity: Official status of Jingjiao temples in Tang China
anchors.notes: Institutional anchor only: it fixes the church's recognised presence empire-wide in 745. No Thomas content.
references: Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937)

anchors.chinese_source: Xi'an (Daqin Jingjiao) Stele, erected at the Daqin temple, Chang'an; composed by Jingjing (Adam)
anchors.event: Stele erected, recording the Jingjiao church's history in China from 635 to 781 and naming its clergy in Chinese and Syriac (~70 Syriac names; Catholicos Hnanisho' named)
anchors.firmness_reason: Self-dated inscription; the stone survives (unearthed 1623-1625)
anchors.indian_entity: Church of the East (Jingjiao) mission in China — the eastern carrier of the Thomas tradition
anchors.notes: The stele does NOT name Thomas anywhere. It dates the institution's China history (635-781), not the apostle. The arriving church traced its own apostolic origin to Thomas in its Syriac tradition, but that self-understanding is not a Chinese record of Thomas.
references: Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937)
Nicolini-Zani, Christian Monks on Chinese Soil (2006)

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Nalanda copper plate of Devapala, regnal year 39, found 1921 in the antechamber of Monastery 1, Nalanda (Epigraphia Indica XVII)
anchors.event: At the request of Balaputradeva, Sailendra king of Suvarnadvipa (Srivijaya), who has built a monastery at Nalanda, Devapala grants five named villages for its monks' requisites, the copying of texts, and the upkeep of the vihara
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated royal charter excavated in situ at Nalanda itself; the only uncertainty is Devapala's accession year (c. 810-821 in competing chronologies), which sets the 849-861 window
anchors.notes: Endowment rate: five villages for ONE vihara (~30-60 residents) implies roughly 6-12 monks supported per village — the same order as Yijing's implied 15 per village, and a cross-check against Huili's implied 100 per village. Also a Srivijaya synchronism: Balaputradeva's reign must intersect this window.
references: N. G. Majumdar, Epigraphia Indica XVII, The Nalanda Copper-plate of Devapaladeva

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL pilgrim anchor (Tibetan, non-Chinese): Biography of Dharmasvamin (Chag lo-tsa-ba Chos-rje-dpal), dictated by the pilgrim, tr. Roerich (1959)
anchors.event: Dharmasvamin studies at Nalanda in 1235 for about six months: the site is damaged and largely deserted after the Turushka raids, but two viharas remain serviceable and the aged abbot Rahulasribhadra (over 90) is still teaching a class of about 70 students
anchors.date_raw: Visit dated by the biography's itinerary to 1235 (in India 1234-1236)
anchors.firmness_reason: Near-eyewitness (dictated by the pilgrim to his biographer); the small numbers are non-round and circumstantial (70 students, a named teacher, a dated raid scare) — the most credible population data point in the whole series, at the series' end
anchors.notes: His hearsay memory of Nalanda's former extent — 7 temples, 14 large and 84 small monasteries — is graded rhetoric in the stats file (84 is a canonical number), but the 70 students is a count, not a trope. Refutes the textbook claim of total destruction c. 1193-1200: the institution was wounded, not annihilated, and teaching continued four decades on.
references: George Roerich (tr.), Biography of Dharmasvamin (1959), with A. S. Altekar's introduction
Biography of Dharmasvamin, Tibetan text ed. Roerich

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (646) and Huili, Life of Xuanzang — attribution of the founding vihara to King Shakraditya; corroborated on the ground by Gupta royal clay sealings excavated in Monastery 1, Nalanda (EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor, non-Chinese)
anchors.event: Nalanda's first royal vihara is founded under Kumaragupta I (Xuanzang's Shakraditya); clay sealings of the Gupta royal line and of the Nalanda sangha were excavated in Monastery 1, physically anchoring the foundation tradition in the Gupta period
anchors.firmness_reason: Shakraditya = Kumaragupta I is an identification, not a naming in any inscription; but the excavated Gupta sealings put royal Gupta patronage on the site in exactly this window
anchors.notes: Xuanzang's own chronology for Shakraditya ('not long after the Buddha's nirvana') is worthless; the identification rests on the sealings and the six-king building sequence in Huili. Conventional founding date c. 427 CE falls inside this reign window. Faxian (c. 410) saw only a village and stupa at Nalanda — a negative attestation just before the window opens.
references: Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Nalanda chapter
Hirananda Sastri, Nalanda and its Epigraphic Material (1942)

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Ghosrawa (Ghosrawan) stone inscription, time of Devapala (Indian Antiquary XVII, 1888)
anchors.event: Viradeva of Nagarahara — trained at the Kaniska vihara near Peshawar, resident at Yasovarmanapura vihara — is elected by the sangha, under Devapala's patronage, to preside over the monasteries of Nalanda, and builds a vihara and chaityas at Ghosrawa
anchors.date_raw: Undated; reign of Devapala, palaeography late 9th century (Fleet)
anchors.firmness_reason: Undated inscription; the window is Devapala's reign widened by Fleet's palaeographic judgement (latter half of the 9th century). Content — a royally backed abbatial appointment — is not in doubt
anchors.notes: Governance anchor: in the later 9th century Nalanda still has a sangha that elects its head and a Pala king who backs the appointment. No population figure.
references: J. F. Fleet, Indian Antiquary XVII (1888), Ghosrawa Buddhist Inscription
Bhagwant Sahai, The Inscriptions of Bihar (1983)

anchors.chinese_source: Huili (completed by Yancong), Life of Xuanzang (Da Ci'en Si Sanzang Fashi Zhuan), presented c. 688
anchors.event: Huili's biography states that Nalanda's residents and visitors together 'always reach 10,000', with about 100 lecture pulpits daily, 1,000 men able to explain twenty collections, 500 able to explain thirty, and Harsa's endowment of about 100 villages with 200 supplying householders each
anchors.firmness_reason: This record anchors the CLAIM's first carrier, not the population: the figure is a disciple's panegyric, is ~3x both Xuanzang's own text and Yijing's eyewitness count, and exceeds the excavated residential plant's capacity by 5-15x (see nalanda/NALANDA-STATS.md capacity test)
anchors.notes: Modern '1,500 faculty' is a sum of Huili's 1,000 + 500 mastery tiers; '2,000 teachers' has no pre-modern carrier at all. Huili's architectural data (eight halls) agree with Yijing exactly — the inflation is specific to crowds, not buildings.
references: Beal, The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang (1911), Nalanda description
Li Rongxi, The Life of Xuanzang (1995)

anchors.chinese_source: Hyecho (Silla), Wang Ocheonchukguk Jeon (Memoir of the Pilgrimage to the Five Kingdoms of India), Dunhuang manuscript
anchors.event: The Korean pilgrim Hyecho passes through Magadha in 723-728 and names Nalanda among its living monasteries; he gives no population figure — a dated presence attestation between Yijing and the Yasovarman inscription
anchors.firmness_reason: Eyewitness itinerary, but the surviving Dunhuang scroll is fragmentary (first volume and end of third lost) and his Nalanda notice is brief; value is chronological, not statistical
anchors.notes: Negative-statistical value: the one 8th-century pilgrim who might have updated the population series gives no number, so the series jumps from Yijing (685) to epigraphy.
references: Yang Han-sung et al., The Hye Ch'o Diary (1984)
Dunhuang manuscript P.3532, Bibliotheque nationale de France

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (compiled 646), Nalanda chapter
anchors.event: Xuanzang resides at Nalanda under abbot Silabhadra; his own Records put the resident priests at 'several thousand', describe eight halls inside one brick wall, and give the gatekeeper's failure rate for would-be debaters as seven or eight in ten
anchors.firmness_reason: Eyewitness resident, but his population figure is an uncounted round phrase ('several thousand'); his architectural count (eight halls) is corroborated independently by Yijing
anchors.notes: The famous 10,000 figure is NOT in this text — it is in Huili's biography (see nalanda-huili-ten-thousand-claim). Xuanzang's own number is consistent with Yijing's 3,000+ a generation later.
references: Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), vol. II, Nalanda chapter
Da Tang Xiyu Ji, fascicle IX

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Nalanda stone inscription of the reign of Yasovarman of Kanauj, found in the southern verandah debris of Monastery 1 (Epigraphia Indica XX, no. 2)
anchors.event: Malada, son of Yasovarman's minister Tikina ('Lord of the North'), makes a permanent endowment (aksaya-nivi) to Baladitya's temple at Nalanda funding daily distribution of rice, curds and ghee to the monks — the mahavihara is endowed and feeding a resident sangha under Kanauj's king
anchors.date_raw: Reign of Yasovarman of Kanauj; the date as read ('731' of an unspecified era) does not convert cleanly
anchors.firmness_reason: The inscription is physically in situ at Nalanda and its content is unambiguous; only its era attribution is disputed, so the window is Yasovarman's reign rather than a single year
anchors.notes: No head-count is given — a provisions anchor, not a population one. The donor's father bears the Turkic title Tikina (tegin), a nice datum for Nalanda's Central Asian connections in the 8th century.
references: Hirananda Sastri, Epigraphia Indica XX (1929-30), pp. 37-46
Bhagwant Sahai, The Inscriptions of Bihar (1983)

anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (Record of Buddhist Practices, sent home 691) and his Memoir of eminent monks
anchors.event: Yijing resides ten years at Nalanda and reports, as an administrator of monastic routine: more than 3,000 resident monks (Memoir: 3,500), eight halls, more than 300 apartments, and landed endowment of more than 200 villages accumulated from successive kings
anchors.date_raw: Tang, Xianheng to Chuigong eras; residence 673-685, Record sent home Tianshou 2 (691)
anchors.firmness_reason: Eyewitness with an administrative (not panegyric) register; his 300 apartments match the excavated ground-floor cell estimate (~250-320) and his 15 monks-per-village ratio is internally consistent with the Devapala plate's endowment rate — the dataset's anchor population witness
anchors.notes: Some manuscripts of the Record read 5,000 for the resident count; Takakusu judged 3,000 the correct reading. Even 3,000 exceeds the excavated core's design capacity (~450-650 cells), so his figure implies the unexcavated remainder of the walled complex and/or shared occupancy — see the capacity test.
references: Takakusu, A Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago (1896)
Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, T.2125

anchors.chinese_source: Ayuwang zhuan (T.2042), translated by An Faqin (fl. 281-306); re-translated as Ayuwang jing (T.2043) by Sanghabhara, 512
anchors.event: The Ashoka legend cycle (84,000 stupas, Upagupta frame, gift-of-dirt prophecy) exists in Chinese translation by c. 306 CE - a TAQ for the legend stratum as formed literature; the cycle's internal frame places Ashoka ~100 years after the parinirvana (the short interval)
anchors.firmness_reason: The translation and its attribution are consistent across the catalogues; An Faqin's exact working years are a floruit, not a colophon year
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 Build A1: bounds the Ashoka-legend stratum, not Ashoka. The short (100-year) nirvana interval rides in this cargo; the long (218-year) interval rides in the Samantapasadika (trans. 488). Neither interval is independent of its lineage.
references: Strong, The Legend of King Ashoka (1983)

anchors.chinese_source: Samantapasadika (T.1462), translated by Sanghabhadra at Canton, 488 CE
anchors.event: Buddhaghosa's Theravada Vinaya commentary - the carrier of the Ceylon 218-year nirvana-to-Ashoka interval - is translated into Chinese in 488; its translator Sanghabhadra is the same monk who placed the 975th dot of the dotted record at Canton in 489 (Campaign 1 case 1)
anchors.firmness_reason: Translation date is catalogue/colophon record; the identity of the dotted record's Sanghabhadra with the translator is the standard reading
anchors.indian_entity: Samantapasadika (Buddhaghosa's Vinaya commentary; Ceylon chronicle arithmetic)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 Build A1: the 218-year interval and the dotted record enter China through the same man in consecutive years - the dependence graded in Campaign 1 case 1 made biographical.

anchors.chinese_source: Fei Changfang, Lidai Sanbao Ji (T.2034), completed 597 CE
anchors.event: Fei's catalogue records several mutually inconsistent backward-counting scales for the Buddha's dates (death dates derivable as early as 1005 BCE) and its own imperial chronology opens with the Buddha's birth in 687 BCE (King Zhuang of Zhou, jiawu year); the rival Zhao/Mu scheme (birth c. 1027 BCE in King Zhao's reign, death c. 949 BCE in King Mu's 52nd year) circulated via the lost Zhou Shu Yiji cited in court debate
anchors.firmness_reason: Firm as a record of what the catalogue says; CONTESTED-to-excluded as evidence for the Buddha's dates - the schemes are Chinese constructions (mofa countdown arithmetic and huahu polemic), mutually inconsistent by up to ~350 years, and all centuries earlier than every Indian-side candidate
anchors.indian_entity: Buddha's birth and parinirvana (Chinese traditional dating)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 Build A2 verdict: CORRECTED in the reverse direction - carried in the tool precisely so the 'Chinese traditional date of the Buddha' cannot be cited as an independent witness.
references: Zanning, Da Song Seng Shi Lue (999)

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Aihole prashasti of Pulakesin II, composed by Ravikirti, dated Saka 556
anchors.event: Ravikirti's prashasti, dated 634 CE, already names Kalidasa (with Bharavi) as a byword for poetic fame - Kalidasa is classical before 634; the same inscription claims Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated royal inscription; the Saka-era conversion is standard and the Kalidasa/Bharavi reference is in the published text
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 Build C5: added because the campaign brief described this TAQ as 'already in the spine' - it was not in anchors.json (checked 2026-11-17). Flagged external on the Gondophares/Quilon precedent. Chinese-translation evidence for Kalidasa: none (no kavya in any Tang catalogue).
references: Aihole prashasti of Pulakesin II (Epigraphia Indica VI)

anchors.chinese_source: Shiji ch. 123 (Account of Dayuan), preserving Zhang Qian's report to Emperor Wu
anchors.date_raw: Zhang Qian returns to Chang'an, Yuanshuo 3 (126 BCE); mission dispatched 138 BCE
anchors.event: Zhang Qian reports Shendu (India) at second hand: in Daxia (Bactria) he saw Shu cloth and Qiong bamboo staffs and was told merchants bought them in Shendu, several thousand li southeast of Daxia, whose people ride elephants to war beside a great river. He never entered India. Shu goods were already reaching Bactria via India before any Han mission
anchors.firmness_reason: The report is preserved in the Shiji with the mission's dated frame (138-126 BCE); its content about India is explicitly hearsay, and is graded as hearsay
anchors.indian_entity: Shendu / India (first Chinese notice; Shu-Shendu-Bactria trade)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D1: the spine's founding record. It dates China's knowledge of India and the trade's existence by c. 128 BCE - and names no Indian king, place or event. Zero-king content sets the channel's pattern from its first page.
references: Yang Juping, The Relations Between China and India and the Opening of the Southern Silk Road During the Han Dynasty

anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu (Tianzhu account); Cefu Yuangui embassy records
anchors.event: Wang Xuance's second mission (dispatched 647) arrives to find Harsha dead and the usurper Arunasa on the throne; the mission is attacked; Wang escapes to Tibet, returns in 648 with 7,000 Nepalese horse and Tibetan troops, defeats Arunasa in a three-day battle, and brings him captive to Chang'an
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic embassy sequence dated at every step; no Indian source records the usurpation at all. The usurper's equation with an Indian 'Arjuna' is probable, not firm, and is graded separately in the case file
anchors.indian_entity: Arunasa's usurpation and defeat (Harsha's succession crisis)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D3: distinct from Campaign 1 case 8 (Harsha's death date). This record grades the succession event, which Indian history does not contain.

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Maharashtra chapter); presented 646
anchors.event: Xuanzang visits Maharashtra and describes its reigning king (Pulakesin II, unnamed in the text): far-reaching in his plans, obeyed by his vassals - and records that Siladitya (Harsha), who had mustered the forces of the five Indies against him, could not subdue him
