anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness residence; the king is identified as Pulakesin II from the Indian side (the Aihole prashasti's Harsha-victory claim, 634), so the corroboration attaches to the frame - an unconquered Deccan king c. 641 - at probable
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D4: the Chinese witness independently attests the substance of the Aihole claim (Harsha checked by the Deccan king) a few years after the inscription; neither source dates the defeat itself (standard dating c. 618-619 is Indian-side).
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Maharashtra chapter

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Kamarupa chapter) and his biography (Huili)
anchors.event: Xuanzang is invited to Kamarupa, resides about a month with King Bhaskaravarman, and is escorted by him to Harsha's Kannauj assembly (643) - a dated eyewitness floruit for the king
anchors.firmness_reason: Pilgrim eyewitness with a dated itinerary; the king is named in the record (unlike the Gupta case), so the synchronism is direct, graded probable only because the month-level dates are itinerary reconstructions
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D5, first half: against an Indian side whose Kamarupa records (Nidhanpur plates) carry no absolute date, the pilgrim's visit is a fixed point in the reign.
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Kamarupa chapter

anchors.chinese_source: Tang records of the Wang Xuance campaign (Jiu/Xin Tang shu; Cefu Yuangui tradition)
anchors.event: After the 648 victory over Arunasa, Bhaskaravarman supplies Wang Xuance's force with cattle, horses and provisions (the Tang tradition gives 30,000 head of cattle) - the king still reigning and cooperative in 648; the same record complex preserves his request for a portrait of Laozi and a translation of the Daodejing
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic logistics record; the Laozi-image request is famous but rests on the same record complex, so both halves are graded probable
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D5, second half: with the 642-643 eyewitness, brackets Bhaskaravarman's attested floruit to 642-648 from two independent Chinese directions.
references: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu and Kamarupa material

anchors.chinese_source: Tang court record (Cefu Yuangui), Kaiyuan 8
anchors.event: Embassy from the king of South India, transcribed Che-li-Na-lo-seng-kia pao-to-pa-mo (Sri Narasimha Potavarman = Narasimhavarman II, Pallava of Kanchi): he offers his elephants and cavalry against the Arabs (Ta-che) and Tibetans (T'ou-po), asks the emperor to name his army and a temple he has built for the emperor; Xuanzong names the army 'the army which cherished virtue' (Huai-de) and the temple Guihua si, and sends a return embassy conferring a brevet title on the king
anchors.firmness_reason: Court record with a reign-era date to the month; the name transcription is phonetically transparent and the identification with Narasimhavarman II is the standard reading (Sastri). The popular claim that the embassy was 'led by Vajrabodhi' is Sastri's inference and is NOT in the record
anchors.indian_entity: Narasimhavarman II, Pallava of Kanchi (embassy to Tang)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D6: a named Pallava king on his throne in a dated Chinese court record, independently confirming the inscriptional reign bracket (c. 700-728). The temple named by the emperor is plausibly - not provably - the Nagapattinam vihara later called the China Pagoda.
references: Sastri, The Colas / Foreign Notices of South India
Mahalingam, Readings in South Indian History

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Magadha / Mahabodhi chapter)
anchors.event: Xuanzang describes the great Sinhalese monastery north of the Bodhi tree (three storeys, six halls, over 1,000 Sthavira monks) standing in 637, and transmits its foundation tradition: a king of Ceylon sent gifts to the Indian emperor and obtained permission to build it for Sinhalese pilgrims. Neither king is named in his text
anchors.firmness_reason: The monastery's existence in 637 is eyewitness (firm as observation); the foundation story is received tradition recorded by the pilgrim, and the named pairing Meghavarna-Samudragupta is a scholarly join with the Allahabad prashasti's Simhala missions, not a statement of either source
anchors.indian_entity: Mahabodhi Sangharama (Sinhalese monastery at Bodh Gaya; Meghavarna embassy tradition)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case D7: bounds the monastery (standing by 637) and corroborates the event class (a Ceylon embassy obtained a Gupta emperor's building permission); it does not date Samudragupta, whose frame is the Gupta era's own.
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Mahabodhi chapter

anchors.chinese_source: Dirghagama (T.1), sutra 27 (Shamenguo jing), read out by Buddhayasas, translated by Zhu Fonian, Chang'an; second recension in Yijing's Mulasarvavastivada Vinaya Sanghabhedavastu (T.1450), 710
anchors.date_raw: Later Qin, Hongshi era (translation completed 413 CE)
anchors.event: The six sramana teachers - Purana Kassapa, Makkhali Gosala, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccayana, Sanjaya Belatthiputta, Nigantha Nataputta (Mahavira) - are preserved as a fixed list with fixed one-line doctrines in the Sramanyaphala-sutra as translated into Chinese in 413 CE: a TAQ for the six-teachers stratum as fossilised syllabus material
anchors.firmness_reason: The Dirghagama translation date (412-413) is catalogue/colophon record; the bound applies to the textual stratum, not to the teachers' floruits, which rest on the Buddha-synchronism of tradition class
anchors.indian_entity: The six sramana teachers (Purana, Gosala, Ajita, Pakudha, Sanjaya, Nigantha Nataputta)
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case E2: carried so the tool records the distinction this campaign insists on - China dates the list, not the men. Mahavira's own interval is chained to the Buddha result (MAHAVIRA.md E1), not derived from this record.

anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Pundravardhana and Samatata chapters; India taxonomy juan 2); record presented 646
anchors.event: Xuanzang counts the naked Nirgranthas (Jains) as the most numerous non-Buddhist sectaries at Pundravardhana and again at Samatata, and describes the order from observation (naked, hair-plucking, cracked skin) - a dated eyewitness snapshot of Jain communities thriving across Bengal eleven centuries after Mahavira
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation, the spine's zero-lag class; graded probable because the pilgrim's 'most numerous' is an impression, not a census, and the Ni-kien = Nirgrantha = Jain identification, though standard, is an identification
anchors.notes: Campaign 2 case E3: pins the order's survival and distribution in the 7th century; says nothing about its origins. No anchor is offered for Mahavira himself, Parsva, Gosala or the Buddha's teachers - the Chinese record dates none of them (MAHAVIRA.md E1, E4-E6).
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Pundravardhana / Samatata chapters
Beal, Si-yu-ki (Buddhist Records of the Western World)

aliases: Yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po
anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL Tibetan anchor: Tengyur, Toh 4310 (with Candranandana's commentary), translation of the later-diffusion (phyi dar) period
anchors.event: Vagbhata's Astangahrdaya — the one great medical samhita the Tibetan canon took — is translated into Tibetan in the translation enterprise associated with Rinchen Zangpo (958-1055)
anchors.date_raw: Later diffusion period, Rinchen Zangpo's lifetime
anchors.firmness_reason: The Tengyur inclusion is certain; the precise translation date and team rest on the colophon tradition of the phyi dar period
anchors.notes: The loosest of Vagbhata's three foreign brackets (Yijing 691 and the Firdaws 850 both bite earlier) — but the socially largest: this translation is why the Hrdaya, not Caraka or Susruta, became Tibet's Ayurveda.
references: Vogel, Vagbhata's Astangahrdayasamhita: the First Five Chapters of its Tibetan Version (1965)

anchors.indian_entity: Early Ayurvedic formulary tradition (Navanitaka; Caraka/Susruta/Bhela-line material)
anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL physical anchor (non-Chinese record): birch-bark manuscript in Gupta script, excavated from a stupa near Kucha (Xinjiang), now Bodleian MS Sansk. c.17
anchors.event: Three of the Bower Manuscript's seven treatises are medical; the Navanitaka formulary opens with a recipe that also stands in the Caraka Samhita and excerpts Caraka-, Susruta- and Bhela-line material
anchors.date_raw: Palaeographic dating (Gupta script; letter ya forms); no radiocarbon published
anchors.firmness_reason: Palaeographic range (Sander 500-550; Callewaert c. 450; Hoernle's final view 4th-5th c.); a published radiocarbon date would make it firm
anchors.notes: A TAQ for the formulary SYSTEM behind the samhitas, not for any one samhita's final form: by c. 500 the eight-branch corpus was mature and excerptable on the Silk Road.

anchors.chinese_source: Da zhuangyan lun jing (Sutralankara, T.201), Chinese translation attributed to Kumarajiva's bureau, Chang'an
anchors.event: The Chinese Sutralankara tells of Kaniska's court attended by the minister Mathara, the bodhisattva Asvaghosa, the minister Devadharma and the physician Caraka — the earliest datable carrier of the tradition that Caraka was Kaniska's physician (identified by Sylvain Levi, 1896)
anchors.date_raw: Later Qin, Hongshi era (Kumarajiva's Chang'an translation activity)
anchors.firmness_reason: T.201's attribution to Kumarajiva is traditional catalogue evidence, and the passage dates the TRADITION, not the redactor: the story is attested ~250 years after the event it claims
anchors.notes: Combined with the Kaniska epoch bound (c. 125-165, Campaign Case 2), the tradition if granted puts the Caraka redaction layer in the mid-2nd c. CE. 'Caraka' may name a school or professional type; the identification is unprovable from this carrier alone.
references: Sylvain Levi, Journal Asiatique (1896), on the Sutralankara's Kaniska court
Meulenbeld, History of Indian Medical Literature IA (1999)

anchors.indian_entity: Organised charitable medicine in India (Pataliputra dispensaries)
anchors.chinese_source: Faxian, Foguo Ji (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), Pataliputra chapter
anchors.event: Faxian, resident in Pataliputra, describes houses established by Vaisya elders for dispensing charity and medicine: the destitute and diseased attend, physicians examine them, and food and medicine are provided free
anchors.date_raw: Faxian's Indian sojourn; three years resident in Pataliputra
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated eyewitness describing what he saw in the city he lived in; the spine's standard pilgrim grade at its strongest
anchors.notes: An infrastructure anchor: dates no text, but proves institutional, physician-staffed charitable medicine in a major Indian city within Drdhabala's floruit window (300-500).
references: Faxian, Foguo Ji, tr. Legge (1886), ch. on Pataliputra

anchors.indian_entity: Indian medical books in Arabic (Sharaka, Susrud, Ashtankar)
anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist, compiled 987-988, discourse on the ancient sciences
anchors.event: The Fihrist catalogues the Indian medical books available in Arabic — Sharaka (Caraka), Susrud (Susruta, tr. Mankha), the Nidana, a book on poisons by Shanaq, and the Ashtankar — most plausibly Vagbhata's Astanga work in Arabic dress
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated catalogue of books its compiler handled; the Ashtankar identification is the one debated element and is corroborative only, the Firdaws (850) attestation of the Hrdaya being earlier and firmer
anchors.notes: The bibliographic terminus of the Barmakid translation movement: by 987 the Ayurvedic canon was a catalogued section of Arabic medicine.

anchors.indian_entity: The Ayurvedic canon in Arabic (Caraka, Susruta, Madhavanidana, Astangahrdaya)
anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ali ibn Rabban al-Tabari, Firdaws al-Hikma (Paradise of Wisdom), completed c. 850, part VII
anchors.event: Al-Tabari closes his medical encyclopedia with a 36-chapter summary of Indian medicine drawn from four named books: Charaka (Jarak), Susruta (Susrud), the Nidana (Niddin = Madhavakara's Rugviniscaya) and the Astangahrdaya (Ashtanqahrada)
anchors.date_raw: Composed at the court of al-Mutawakil, c. 849-850
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated, extant work; Meyerhof's identification of the four Arabic titles with the four Sanskrit works is the standard reading (Isis 16, 1931; Siggel's 1951 edition of the Indian chapters)
anchors.notes: One dated page brackets four canon texts at once: Caraka, Susruta, Madhava (c. 700) and Vagbhata's Hrdaya all existed in Arabic-accessible form by 850. The earliest datable Arabic attestation of Caraka's content.
references: Siggel, Die indischen Bucher aus dem Paradies der Weisheit (1951)

anchors.indian_entity: Indian oculist practising in China (golden-scalpel cataract couching)
anchors.chinese_source: Liu Yuxi (772-842), poem 'Presented to the Brahmin Monk Eye-Doctor' (Zeng yanyi poluomen seng), with the companion reply poem of winter 837
anchors.event: Liu Yuxi, himself medically literate, addresses the Indian Brahmin monk whose golden-scalpel art is to lift his three years of blindness; a dated companion poem of winter 837 celebrates the cure — 'the golden scalpel is no longer needed'
anchors.date_raw: Tang, Kaicheng 2 winter (837) for the cure poem
anchors.firmness_reason: The poems are datable only through Liu Yuxi's biography and Pei Du's Luoyang tenure; the 837 companion poem anchors the cure, the address poem itself may be slightly earlier
anchors.notes: The signature operation of the Susruta tradition, performed on a named, datable Chinese patient in the 830s — the transmission at the level of the individual practitioner's hands.
references: Quan Tang Shi, Liu Yuxi poems

anchors.indian_entity: Indian physician at the Tang court (Narayanasvamin's longevity drug)
anchors.chinese_source: Jiu Tang Shu (Tianzhu account) and Zizhi Tongjian, s.a. 648-649
anchors.event: Wang Xuance's returning mission brings the Magadhan brahmin Narayanasvamin to Chang'an; under Taizong's patronage he compounds a longevity drug — the emperor dies in 649, and the annalists leave the elixir beside the death
anchors.firmness_reason: Annalistic record of a named foreign specialist at court; the elixir episode is told with a moralising edge, so the fact of the commission is firmer than its pharmacology
anchors.notes: Dates Indian medicine's prestige at the Tang throne, not any text. Gaozong's reign adds the East Indian monk-physician Lokaditya, sent to gather drugs from the southern seas.

anchors.indian_entity: Indian formulary material in China (Jivaka prescriptions; Brahmin massage method)
anchors.chinese_source: Sun Simiao, Beiji Qianjin Yaofang (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold), completed 652
anchors.event: Sun Simiao's dated formulary incorporates Indian material under Indian names: formulas attributed to Jivaka (incl. the Jivaka myriad-disease pill), a Jivaka saying traced to Caraka Samhita Sutrasthana 26.12 ('nothing in the world is not a medicine'), and the 'Brahmin method' of massage with the eighteen postures of Tianzhu
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated, extant Chinese compilation citing its Indian material by name; the Caraka line arrives under Jivaka's attribution, which is why the record is firm for Indian formulary circulation and only indirect for Caraka's text
anchors.notes: The eastward channel in one record: Ayurveda reached China as attributed formulas and body practices inside Chinese books, not as translated samhitas.
references: Unschuld, Medicine in China: A History of Pharmaceutics (1986)

anchors.indian_entity: Indian medical literature in Chinese translation (Brahmin pharmacopoeias, Nagarjuna pharmacopoeia, Jivaka formulas)
anchors.chinese_source: Sui shu, Jingji zhi (bibliographic treatise), medical section
anchors.event: The Sui imperial bibliography lists eleven Indian medical titles in Chinese dress, incl. Pharmacopeia of the Brahmin Rsis (20 juan), Brahmin Pharmacopeia (5 juan), Pharmacopeia of Nagarjuna Bodhisattva (4 juan), Essential Formulas of Famous Physicians of the Western Regions (4 juan), Jivaka's Formulas (2 juan) — most inherited from the Liang imperial catalogue
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated imperial catalogue entry is the spine's standard firm existence proof; the titles themselves are lost, so it dates a transmission, not contents
anchors.notes: What it does NOT list matters equally: no Caraka and no Susruta translation is recorded here or in any Chinese bibliography — the great samhitas never entered China as books. The Nagarjuna of the pharmacopoeia is the medical/alchemical namesake, not evidence about the Madhyamika.
references: Deshpande, 'Glimpses of Ayurveda in Medieval Chinese Medicine', Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008)

anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist (987), on the Barmakid translation movement
anchors.event: The Fihrist records that Mankha (Manka), an Indian physician at the Abbasid court, translated Susruta from Sanskrit into Arabic for the vizier Yahya ibn Khalid al-Barmaki
anchors.date_raw: Yahya ibn Khalid's vizierate under Harun al-Rashid, ended by the Barmakid fall
anchors.firmness_reason: The translation is recorded in a dated catalogue two centuries later; Mankha's presence at Harun's court is independently remembered (he is said to have cured the caliph), but no colophon of the translation itself survives
anchors.notes: Susruta existed, complete enough to translate whole, by 803 at the latest — three centuries after the internal evidence closes its present form. A confirmation anchor, not a tightening one.
references: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, tr. Dodge (1970), chapter on Indian medicine

anchors.indian_entity: Susruta Samhita, complete six-book text (oldest dated manuscript)
anchors.chinese_source: EXTERNAL physical anchor (non-Chinese record): palm-leaf manuscript, Kaiser Library, Kathmandu, MS KL 699
anchors.event: The oldest surviving manuscript of the Susruta Samhita, dated by its colophon era to 878 CE, already contains the complete text including the Uttaratantra
anchors.firmness_reason: The 878 date rests on the reading of the manuscript's colophon era; the manuscript's completeness is directly inspectable
anchors.notes: A physical TAQ for the FINISHED Susruta: whatever the layers' dates, the six-book whole existed in this form by 878 — comfortably after the internal c. 500 closure and before Dalhana's commentary (c. 1200).
references: Meulenbeld, HIML IA (1999), on the Susruta manuscript tradition

anchors.indian_entity: Indian ophthalmology and Jivaka formulary in China (Tianzhu eye treatise; golden-scalpel couching)
anchors.chinese_source: Wang Tao, Waitai Miyao (Secret Essentials of an Official), completed 752, juan 21 (eye diseases) and passim
anchors.event: Wang Tao's dated formulary (6,900 prescriptions, sources named) carries Jivaka-attributed remedies throughout, and its eye section opens with the Preface to the Indian (Tianzhu) Treatise on Eyes by Master Xie of Longshang, who received the doctrine from a Western monk — followed by the first detailed Chinese account of golden-scalpel cataract couching
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated, extant compilation that names its sources; the Indian provenance of the eye treatise is stated by its Chinese transmitter himself
anchors.notes: Indian ophthalmology existed as a TEXT in China by 752. A large share of all Indian-derived prescriptions preserved in Chinese literature is concentrated in this one book (Fan's count).
references: Fan Ka Wai, and Deshpande, Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008)

anchors.indian_entity: Indian ('Brahmin') prescription in the Tang imperial pharmacopoeia
anchors.chinese_source: Su Jing et al., Xinxiu Bencao (Newly Revised Materia Medica), imperial commission, 659
anchors.event: The Tang state pharmacopoeia records a 'Brahmin's prescription' as the known remedy for beriberi (jiaoqi), in all probability carried to China by an Indian Buddhist monk
anchors.firmness_reason: A dated imperial pharmacopoeia entry; the Indian provenance is stated in the record itself
anchors.notes: An Indian formula with official Chinese status by 659 — the transmission at the level of practice, a generation before Yijing's eyewitness account of the system behind it.

anchors.indian_entity: Cikitsavidya (medicine) as a formal Indian science
anchors.chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (646), juan 2, on Indian education
anchors.event: Xuanzang lists the five sciences of the standard Indian curriculum — grammar, crafts, cikitsavidya (the science of medicine), logic and inner science — taught to students across India
anchors.firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness synthesis by the pilgrim who had just spent over a decade studying in India
anchors.notes: Attests medicine's institutional status — a named, teachable sastra — in mid-7th-century India, independent of any single text's date.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, juan 2
tr. Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884)

anchors.indian_entity: Vagbhata's Astanga synthesis (the eight branches epitomised in one work)
aliases: Jin ri you ren lue wei yi jia
anchors.chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (written 691), vol. 3, sections 27-29 (on the origin of disease, on medicine, on harmful drugs)
anchors.event: Yijing, resident in India 673-685, names the eight branches of Indian medicine and reports that they 'formerly existed in eight books, but lately a man has compiled them into one fascicle' — the standard scholarly identification of the unnamed epitome is Vagbhata's Astanga synthesis
anchors.firmness_reason: Yijing's text and date are firm and he is a resident eyewitness; the one inferential step is identifying his anonymous 'one fascicle' epitome with Vagbhata's Astanga works (the reading standard since Takakusu)
anchors.notes: The sharpest foreign bracket on Vagbhata anywhere: the synthesis existed by 691 and was recent enough to remark on — pressing the c. 600-650 window from above. Yijing's sections 27-29 are also the fullest dated foreign description of Indian medicine as practised.
references: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, tr. Takakusu (1896), chs. 27-29 and note
J. Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine 20:92 (2024), analysis of the medical chapters
